The house resumed, from Friday, January 27, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for shortterm credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain; to provide also that the governor in council may extend the application of the act to cover loans made before the 1st day of June, 1957; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the act be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of this debate I have attempted to point out a few of the many reasons why this legislation should not be passed. In conclusion I should like to summarize those points which I attempted to make when I last spoke in this debate. Before I do so,

however, may I refer for a few moments to what must surely have seemed like an extremely humorous incident involving the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and a Manitoba farmer's reaction to this legislation. I mention this matter only because of the fact that it has some significance. As far as I am concerned, this man's feelings were quite understandable. I imagine that since last fall he was completely incensed at the injustice of the situation and became further incensed at the proposition the government is putting forth in the form of bank loans to cure that particular situation. So all winter long this man nursed this great and burning sense of wrong. Then, almost at the breaking point, he had the great misfortune of seeing on television the hon. member for Rosthern in an extremely clumsy attempt to justify the government's bank loan legislation. I can imagine with what demon-like glee he reached for his shotgun and in one reckless moment had his revenge, satisfied at last that he had gained some kind of wild justice. I think that all of us in the opposition should take up a collection and buy for this, shall I say, rather impetuous gentleman a new television receiver as a token of our appreciation of his having brought to the attention of this house in a dramatic way what surely must be the inner feelings of the majority of western farmers. As far as the hon. member for Rosthern is concerned, he can take cold comfort from the fact that it was only a television show.
The producers are opposed to this legislation because they see in it an attempt to exact a penalty for the production of food. In other words, they feel that they are being victimized because of the fact that this government has failed to bring in a realistic agricultural policy that would be geared to distribution, not only on the domestic front but in the export market, with respect to the agricultural products that have been produced in this country. The farmers repudiate this legislation on the ground that it did not work in 1951. In the light of present-day conditions they see in it an indication of its utter uselessness, in view of the unfortunate experience in 1951. As to the $1,500 as a maximum loan, they see that as a delusion.
It is just a piece of bait that is being dangled under the noses of western farmers. I suggest to the government that when they attempt this sort of thing on future occasions they should keep in mind the old adage, when you bait a mousetrap be sure to leave room for the mouse. If these are not enough valid reasons why this legislation should be 67509-53i
Grain
rejected, then I suggest to hon. members that the arguments put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce are in themselves the best reason why it should be rejected. To imply, as the minister did, that all those who oppose the legislation do so with the express desire of getting rid of the wheat board-mind you, that opposition includes the western pools, the farm union organizations, the federated co-operatives and many thousands of individual farmers-is a pretty weak argument.
The farmers feel that only by a realistic agricultural policy are they going to be able to obtain for themselves a standard of income comparable with that now being enjoyed by other industries in the country. I agree that farming, as was said by the Minister of Agriculture, is a way of life and it cannot be confused with any other kind of business. In other words, when no profit is forthcoming the farmer still stays in business. That is the difference, but I accuse the government of exploiting that fact to the very limit. The government knows that the farmer will stay in business in order to try to protect the investment of a lifetime even if he knows that at the end of the year he is only going to get the meanest of wages for his work. The government knows the farmer will carry on until he goes under in order to protect that investment.	:
If every farmer stopped producing because his farming operations were not showing a profit today it would mean chaos for the Canadian economy and starvation for most of our people. Yet if the government allows the farmer to go under because they fail to introduce a comprehensive agricultural policy that will put some stability under the industry the whole economy will be dragged down.. The most expensive gesture any government can make, and apparently it is the expensive gesture this government is making, is to believe that our prosperity rests on the manipulations that take place on the stock exchange rather than believing, as they should,, that our prosperity rests on the broad base of our land resources. To think otherwise is a fallacy and one that can only end in disaster.

speechtext: It is reported now that you were the one involved.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend should not be interrupting after the "McCanntics" of last summer. What I want to speak about is the general reaction in western Canada to this legislation. Meetings took place in various cities and towns. There was a suggestion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that I had had something to do with convening the meeting in Prince Albert. Let me say that statement bore about as much resemblance to the truth as some other statements the minister made. As a matter of fact, three of four days before that meeting was convened by representatives of the farmers union, the board of trade and the Prince Albert chamber of commerce, business representatives such as the retail merchants association, I was invited to speak. The total length of time I spoke in a meeting of some three hours in extent represented not more than 10 minutes. Indeed, one of the outstanding Liberal supporters and a very fine gentleman named Mr. James McCarter who I believe is one of the senior members of the Prince Albert Liberal executive, came out strongly in support of the only means whereby anything could be done on behalf of the western farmer, a system of advances on farm stored wheat.
Now, for the life of me I cannot understand the attitude of the government. All kinds of explanations have been given as to why the farmers should not be entitled to this. The first position that was taken was that it could not be done because the elevator agents would not be able to do it. Today the elevator agents are responsible for the collection of whatever moneys are lent by the banks. The farmers in the western provinces find themselves in this position, and I think the analogy is a fair one. What would any labouring man do if, working for a concern, he found himself in a position when he came to collect his wages where the employer would say, "Well, we have not sold the raw products yet. We will guarantee your loan at the bank. We are the only source of payment but we cannot pay you now. You go to the bank and borrow and we will guarantee, up to a certain extent, the 
repayment of that loan." That is the position in which the farmer finds himself under this legislation, substituting one debt for another, substituting a series of debts for one united debt.
So far as this legislation is concerned, it had its birth in a series of statements made by various ministers. Tracing something of the history of this legislation, we find the first notice we had was when Mr. McDonald, the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan and an estimable gentleman, realizing that the situation was serious, made a pilgrimage to Ottawa. He said his plan was a secret, but it would be revealed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and to the members of the cabinet who were particularly concerned with the marketing of wheat. He went and he carried that secret in his soul. He revealed it to the cabinet. Two or three days later he was able to return to Saskatchewan and say, in effect, "Eureka, I have got it."
Well, it was the old, old loan scheme of 1951, decorated up a little, polished over and reburnished. This scheme did not work, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has so often said. Now, when the first announcement was made that the loan scheme was going to be the one, Mr. McDonald, with true powers of statesmanlike perception, said, "This thing will be just as helpful as a stirrup pump against a forest fire." Today the stirrup pump has become the cornerstone of government policy.
Now, apparently the Minister of Agriculture did not know what government policy was on October 24, for in Winnipeg on that date-

speechtext: I am reading from the record, Mr. Chairman, and there has been no denial at any time except when it becomes convenient to deny a statement made that should not have been made. This was reported in the Free Press and Winnipeg Tribune. The minister says there are some here who heard. They may have heard but apparently they did not understand.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They understood.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Now, the new scheme that was finally evolved was this loan scheme. Now, what kind of scheme is this? What is the purpose of it? The people in western Canada are aroused. The farmers are annoyed at this time. The only western people who are in favour of it so far as I am able to ascertain, and I have spoken with a great many, are those who are bound to this government. The wheat pool in Saskatchewan came out in favour of cash advances. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) sent a resolution from his association and the other day, amidst what Hansard records as a considerable clatter, he endeavoured to distinguish between an advance and a loan, much to his own discomfiture.
Now, sir, what is this scheme? What is this loan scheme? Well, the doctors have what they call a placebo. It is an inactive medicine prescribed to quieten a patient, to neutralize opposition. It is a harmless substance given to soothe a patient's anxiety rather than as a remedy. It is a preparation given to silence or temporarily satisfy a patient. It is something intended to soothe. This is the government's placebo, but it has not done what it was intended to do, to soothe the aroused feelings of western farmers.
What information have we regarding the success or failure of this plan? I cannot understand answers like these. They seem to emanate generally from the Department of Trade and Commerce. I asked a simple question. It is answered as No. 12. The questions were:
1.	How many bank loans on farm-stored grain subject to government guarantees have been applied for in each province, week by week, since the inception of the plan in November last?
2.	Of the said applications, how many have been turned down or refused?
3.	What is the total amount loaned in each province to date?
Grain
The answer to questions 1 and 2 is as follows:
As applications are made to chartered banks, the government has no record of the number of loans applied for and the number turned down or refused.
Up to November 30 the loans under this scheme amounted to $2,500,000.
Up to November 30, Mr. Chairman; why did we not get the information up to December 30 or up to January 15? Why is it that the information given the other day was so restrictive and circumscribed? The reason is that this plan has been a total flop so far as the western farmer is concerned. It has not worked; it will not work. It is not supplying money to the western farmers. Farmers are being turned down by the banks on every hand when they do apply. If their normal credit is not sufficient, time after time they find themselves turned down. They are asked what the purpose is in securing the money, and if they give as the reason that they have in mind the payment of certain accounts, in many instances the answer immediately is: "That is not what this loan plan is for."

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is making statements about the lending policy of the banks. I think he should prove his statement by specific instances. If the banks are doing that, they are violating the agreement with the government. I do not believe my hon. friend knows many farmers. He talks for the city.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am making this statement in this house as a responsible member responsible to the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: In very vague terms.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have example after example. Let me make it clearer. Your scheme is a complete flop.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: In your opinion. You did not understand it before.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Some people think you are a complete flop.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Since the Minister of Agriculture has spoken, let me give him one. I suppose he will deny this. He was explaining why the government had not acted, and he said: "The mills of the government grind slowly". It used to be the mills of the gods.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, if I made the statement that is what I would have said.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Does the government say today these two terms are synonymous? Sometimes we agree, Mr. Chairman.

Grain
I now want to deal particularly with one of the major reasons why the farmer is not getting funds.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You would not know why he is not.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
These are the types of interruptions that indicate the attitude of the minister to the western farmer.
Let me deal with some of the records in so far as the marketings are concerned. Here are the actual figures that cannot be contradicted. I am going to deal first with marketings in the prairie provinces. Let me compare 1954-55 with 1955-56, up to December 8. In the latter year 50 million fewer bushels were marketed in that period than there were a year ago, and it has been getting worse. The minister said things are improving. Up to January 19 the marketings in the prairie provinces were 75-6 million bushels fewer than they were a year ago. In other words, the total prairie marketings of grain have steadily declined right from the beginning of the crop season, from August 1, down to the present day.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Why was that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment. It was because of the department's failure, firstly, to provide through the controller the necessary freight cars that were available for the purpose. I have the actual statistics now. The minister gave us the figures the other day, but I do not know where he got them. They certainly did not come from the wheat board.
Let us take a look at lakehead stocks. Up to December 8, 1955, as compared with the preceding year, the lakehead stocks were down by 1 [DOT] 9 million bushels. Up to December 14 they had decreased by 9-9 million bushels; up to December 29, they had decreased by 15-3 million bushels; up to January 5, they had decreased by 20-3 million bushels; and up to January 19, by 21-1 million bushels. Lakehead stocks have continued to decrease steadily during the past several months.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is because wheat is being sold.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We will come to that in a second. That is the explanation at the moment, but I shall show shortly what the explanation is.
I now turn to millions of bushels in country elevators. On December 7, 1955-56, there were 23-8 million more bushels of wheat in country elevators than a year ago. That has been reduced. Up to January 19, it had been reduced to 12-9 million.
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]
We now come to the shipments from country elevators. For the week of December 9 we find the shipments were fewer by 3-9 million bushels. That situation was accelerated, until December 28, when shipments amounted to 5-1 million bushels fewer than the preceding year.
The minister mentioned that that situation had been somewhat improved, and very considerably improved lately. Because these facts and figures are unchallengeable I am going to say immediately that up to January 19 of that week there was an improvement. There were 500,000 fewer bushels of wheat in country elevators in 1956 than in 1955.
The cumulative shipments from country elevators are very interesting. Up to December 7, 1955-56, the total number of bushels of wheat shipped from country elevators amounted to 141-7 million bushels. In the previous year the figure was 212-2 million bushels. In other words, the cumulative shipments from country elevators were 71-5 million bushels fewer. What is the position today? On January 19 they had increased. The cumulative shipments from the beginning of the season this year to January 19 amounted to 188-8 million bushels, as compared with 274-6 million a year ago, or 85-8 million fewer. There is your picture. If the farmers had been able to market the same amount of wheat, if the storage facilities had been used -and I emphasize that-if cars had been made available as they should have been, there would have been an improvement. You say the weather had something to do with it. The weather had nothing to do with cars being made available to remove the wheat that was in the elevators in the province of Saskatchewan, or in the line elevators of Alberta or Manitoba.
What about car unloadings? This tells a story of somnolence on the part of the government. Up to December 8, 1954-55, 67,791 cars were unloaded at the lakehead. This year it was only 45,537 or 22,200 less but it got worse week by week since that time and on December 14 for that week there were 24,482 less cars unloaded than the year before. On December 28 there were 27,869 less cars unloaded at the lakehead than a year before. January 25, 29,656 less; and January 19, 30,106 less than a year ago. In other words car unloadings are far below last year's approximately 35 per cent.
The daily average tells a story. The daily average during December and in successive weeks was 201 less than a year ago, 210 less than a year ago, 218 less than a year ago, 219 less than a year ago and up to January 19 it was 203 less per day than a year ago. In other words, we are placed in

Grain
a position where car unloadings have fallen to unequalled depths as compared with a year ago.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that we have increased the number. The average for the last week of January was 867, as I remember it. That is all to the good, but what does that show? I have averaged this out and the average indicates that, even making allowance for what has taken place during the last week of January, this year 31,000 less cars of wheat have been unloaded than a year ago since the beginning of the crop year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend just now analysing the situation and discovering that Canada is short of box cars? I announced that three months ago.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We will come to the question of box cars. I have some statistics from the dominion bureau of statistics indicating that every industry in Canada has had an increase in box cars, but as far as western farmers are concerned there was a tremendous decrease of approximately 35,700 up to January 19. Where has the controller been? He has been away on vacation at a time when a most serious situation faces the western farmers. I say that this reveals a collapse in organization. It indicates that not sufficient attention has been paid to providing cars to the western farmer.
There was space available. I have figures concerning the availability of terminal space. The hon. gentleman said we were all wrong in assuming that there was 100 million bushels of terminal space available. I have taken the rated capacity of the elevators across the country in British Columbia, the prairies, the lakehead and in eastern Canada. Deducting that rated capacity of from 10 per cent to 12 per cent in order to provide for the effective working capacity, accepting the figures which appeared in the wheat board returns, there was available in the month of January at least 95 to 97 million bushels of space that just lay there because of the failure of the government to act in regard to the provision of cars.
I shall read what the Regina Leader-Post said with regard to that on December 27, 1955:
Empty terminal space worthless-
Clearing space in the lakehead and Pacific grain terminals for approximately 97,000,000 bushels of prairie grain should be cheering news for prairie farmers. Deducting the 38,000,000 bushels in transit, this would leave room for approximately 60,000,000 more bushels. If utilized for wheat, this would put something like $85,000,000 more cash into the prairie farmers' pockets. But it will do no good if it stays empty while country elevators remain clogged so that farmers are unable to deliver their grain.
The fact that within a few weeks, this space has developed to the extent it has indicates a grave weakness in our grain handling system. Reports attribute it to a shortage of cars for shipping grain.
The situation smacks at the best of a lack of foresight on the part of those who are in charge of grain handling. At the worst, it has the earmarks of ignoring the prairies and the plight of its farmers who are hard pressed to maintain their families and their operations on the proceeds of the sale of their wheat plus what they are able to borrow from the banks at five per cent interest.
Then it goes on to say this:
Mr. Howe said in Edmonton a few days ago that he had made it plain to the railway companies that there is no higher priority than box cars for grain. Obviously, he did not make this sufficiently plain to get results. This oversight should be rectified immediately.
Here are the two positions which indicate what happens when governments are long in power and when those in charge of departments develop an infallibility belief. There was storage available to the extent of from 90 to 100 million bushels.
I have the record for freight cars indicating that practically every other type of industry has had a tremendous increase in the number of freight cars available to it. Why should the western provinces have been placed in the position, in this regard, of being a depressed area in an otherwise expanding economy? Those are the things in relation to which we have a right to ask what is being done. Why did the controller not act?
I mentioned that I would give certain figures from the dominion bureau of statistics published on January 11, 1956. These figures tell their own story. Loadings in the year 1955 were as follows: Grain, 1955, 333,233 cars; 1954, 364,160 cars. Grain products, 1955, 130,902; 1954, 134,900. Then you take the other elements within the economy and you find tremendous increases in the number of cars made available.
What has happened, Mr. Chairman, has placed the government in the position where they now run for cover and they intimate that anyone who criticizes the situation is thereby inimical to the wheat board. As far as I am concerned I still remember that it was the Conservatives who set up the wheat board and I remember it was the Liberals who set it aside in 1937 and did not restore it until 1942 when they brought it in in order to keep the price of wheat down. Those things I remember-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Your memory is bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Very faulty
indeed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
As far as the wheat board is concerned, a statement was made

Grain
the other day in my absence by my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Jutras) which I must refer to. That statement was to the effect that my attitude was at fault and the hon. member for Prince Albert would fire the wheat board overnight without batting an eye. Mr. Chairman, that statement does not have the degree of truthfulness for which my hon. friend has established such an enviable reputation. That statement bears no relationship to the facts. When I spoke about the wheat board I asked the question, which is not yet answered: why is it that the members of the wheat board said they would not stay on the job if cash advances were provided for? We have not yet had an answer to that question. I asked for the letters that were received. I wonder if they take that attitude. As far as I am concerned the wheat board must remain inviolate and it must stay, but we have a right to ask that the government's tinkering with the wheat board be discontinued.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of the debate last Friday I obtained the idea in some way or another that it was thought to be highly dangerous if members of the opposition group continued to prolong this debate. It was indicated that by doing so we would do more harm than good. I cannot follow that kind of reasoning because it is my opinion that members of this house should be permitted to express themselves freely at all times on any matter that concerns them. This particular question before us surely is of great concern to all hon. members of the house because it deals with the basic roots of the greatest industry in Canada.
It was intimated last Friday as well that if this debate were to continue much longer the farmers of western Canada might panic. I have lived with the farmers of western Canada all my life and I know that they do not panic. Yesterday a newspaper contained a picture of an hon. member with a few comments about the use of a shotgun. I can assure the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) that he or any other hon. member can come out to my constituency and no shotguns will be used. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is fully aware of the fact that the farmers of Alberta can shoot some pretty warm questions when they are concerned. He experienced it at the farmers' union meeting at the Alberta college auditorium in December last year when for 90 minutes the delegates peppered him with questions to which they received answers which did not satisfy them.
Our farmers are used to being treated roughly, as apparently that is their lot in

Canadian society. On Friday the old reciprocity issue of 1911 was dragged across the floor of this house. I thought that skeleton was buried long ago. The farmers of the west were able to get through the days of the depression even though they were on an almost starvation level. They came through the war period. They are true Canadians and they will stick to their guns even though they are not getting what the national economy should provide.
However, they have learned a few lessons throughout the years. They have learned one lesson in particular, that it is only through organized efforts that they have been able to get the few advantages they have obtained.
Some mention has been made of the wheat board, and that we on this side of the house are opposed to the wheat board. I submit that that statement is far from the truth. We have always supported the wheat board and will continue to support it as the years go by. Through their co-operative organizations, through the wheat pools, the united grain growers, the farmers' unions in the three western provinces, our farmers are now presenting a united front which I hope will continue to grow stronger and stronger as the years go by.
The farmers in my area are definitely opposed to the $1,500 5 per cent guaranteed bank loan. They do not like it and I do not believe there are many of them using it. I know for a fact that a few have tried to obtain loans but were refused. I am thinking in terms of a young farmer who applied for the $1,500 bank loan but was refused. Why? He was refused because he had an outstanding debt of $1,600 on a combine, $800 payable this fall and the other $800 payable next fall. His only other debt, besides his store and fuel bills and so on, was a $300 breaking bill. That young man wanted to establish himself as a good farmer but he was unable to get a loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not true that his grain was pledged under section 88 of the Bank Act in connection with his other loans?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
This young man had 5,000 bushels of wheat. What is the history of this so-called bank loan as known to the people down here? We know the history as it has been related to us many times. I have been quite concerned when in the corridors of this building I hear from hon. members who are not directly associated with wheat growing that they are getting sick and tired of hearing about the wheat problem. I can only say that I hope they get so sick

Grain
and tired of listening to the details of that problem that . they will get behind us and support us. The Edmonton Journal of October 19, 1955, contained the following statement as a result of an interview with the Prime Minister:
The cabinet spent the morning discussing the urgent need of getting some cash into the hands of prairie farmers who hold heavy stocks of grain on their farms.
And again:
He brushed off questions about cash advances for farm-held grain, saying Mr. Howe will make the announcement.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce finally made the announcement of a $1,500 guaranteed bank loan to the farmers of the west. Following that announcement a wave of protest swept through Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Protest meetings were called, not by politicians or big businessmen but by farmers, the little fellows on a quarter or half section of land. They got together and protested and they are still protesting about these bank loans. The following statement which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of November 30 seems significant to me:
Ottawa. The federal government is guaranteeing the chartered banks against any foreseeable loss on their wheat loans to western farmers but it is also making assurance doubly sure that there won't be any loss to the treasury.
There seems to be great concern on the part of the federal government that the chartered banks shall not lose any money or that the federal government itself shall not lose any money, but what about the farmers of the west. When they take out a loan they are faced immediately with a 5 per cent reduction in the amount of the income they should receive. The article goes on:
The only thing that will save Mr. Howe from a repetition of last year's defence production bill filibuster is the fact that by the time parliament gets its hands on the issue it will be a fait accompli.
I submit that the issue of surplus wheat disposal, was critical enough last fall to have justified the government in calling a special session of parliament so that this issue could have been fully discussed before it was a fait accompli. In the same statement the following appeared:
The elevator officials-the agents-will make out two payment tickets.
Still we are told in this house that the elevator officials are not capable of doing that in the case of cash advances. This surplus problem is not a new one; it has been with us for years. It became of great concern toward the end of the last crop year. Throughout the early fall the farmers were wondering
how they were going to market their wheat so that they could pay their bills and so on. Through the press we had statements which were issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He blamed all sorts of things for the surplus. He blamed better European crops, scarce ocean shipping and United States surplus disposal methods. He is now blaming the box car situation, the weather and so on. I should like to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that he lay the blame where it belongs, namely on the operation of his own department.
Let us go back to the shortage of box cars. May I ask this question, Mr. Chairman? Who owns the Canadian National Railways, other than the people of Canada? Who subsidizes the Canadian Pacific Railway other than the people of Canada? Surely we should, as a group of people, have something to say about the directing of box cars to where they are needed.
It has already been pointed out by the hon. member for Prince Albert that box cars are apparently plentiful for other branches of industry in Canada, but certainly they are not plentiful so far as agriculture is concerned. Last fall the farmers of my area were permitted to market-if they could find space in the elevators-300 bushels of grain. The income from 300 bushels of grain was certainly not enough to meet the day by day expenses incurred by the farmers of the west, such as fuel bills. I can well recall one farmer showing me a cheque for $413 and, at the same time, a fuel bill for $456. That was a fuel bill only. Grocery bills are unpaid. Taxes to municipal governments and so on were not paid before the last day of discount or are not paid at all. I know of one well-established farmer who, for the first time in his 25 years on the farm, was this year unable to pay his taxes. This situation affects not only the farmers, Mr. Chairman, but it is having its effect in every small community in my part of the province. Its influence is being felt, I submit, even right down here in the east. There is not one small town or village in Alberta through which you can travel and not notice stored up on vacant lots or other places combines and farm equipment of all types which have not been sold. If you go into hardware stores which had been expecting to sell deep-freezes, and other equipment that is badly needed by the farmers in the west, you find it is still there in the stores. The farmers have no money with which to buy it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The government is in a mental deep freeze.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Much has been said, Mr. Chairman, about some of

Grain
the so-called fantastic schemes by which this situation might be cured, such as the adoption of a two-price system by this government, the use of the barter system and so on. May I ask this question, Mr. Chairman? Which is the more fantastic: to attempt some of the schemes used by other respectable nations in this world and get rid of our grain, or to stay away from these so-called fantastic schemes and to see millions of bushels of wheat on the farms of western Canada while at the same time millions of people are starving throughout the world?
I should like to submit, Mr. Chairman, that in the United States of America the farmers are offered $2.08 a bushel for wheat. What does the United States do with this wheat? It gives special deals to importers backed by the federal treasury. In the Argentine the price is $2.72 a bushel; Argentine offers special deals to the importers and accepts barter deals. In France the price is $2.64 per bushel, and the two-price system is used. In Canada the price is $1.40 a bushel. The farmers in Canada are still forced to follow that so-called old system of rugged individualism in this modern age. Australia accepts sterling. I am suggesting that it will not be too long before we in Canada as well are forced to accept sterling.
It has been suggested that the farmers of the west do not want cash advances. May I say that the farmers of the west have asked for cash advances. The Farmers' Union of Alberta in convention early in December passed the following resolution:
Cash advances on farm-stored grain after inspection as to quantities, grade, and condition of storage facilities.
For the life of me, Mr. Chairman, I cannot see why the government is so reluctant to grant this request for cash advances. That is something I just do not understand. However, I know that the $1,500 bank loan will not be used to any great extent. It will certainly not be used by the people, the younger farmers, who actually need it because the banks will not give them the loan without banker's security.
I have before me this resolution. It is a modern one, and I can produce others as well. It was passed by the Farmers' Union of Alberta local in my territory, and it reads as follows:
Resolved that this meeting go on record as being dissatisfied with the federal government's policy on guaranteed bank loans on farm-stored grain. We regard it as completely inadequate and unrealistic in view of the economic situation of the western farmer.
At this particular meeting 72 farmers travelled to a centre over roads that were
[Mr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1
practically impassable. They are concerned and they are determined that something must be done.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. Instead of trying to spend our time in debating something that has already been accomplished-by so doing we are not going to change the course of history-I feel that we should adopt another course. Parliament did not ask for the $1,500 loan. It was the Minister of Trade and Commerce who did that. What has been done is done. There is nothing we can do about it but cry. Instead of wasting our time doing this, I suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should bring forth immediately a definite, longterm policy regarding the marketing of wheat so that we could sit here as a group of legislators and discuss it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not
rising to prolong the debate. I am rising to put forward, as briefly as I can, the position that I think most of us on this side of the house take in relation to the proposal now before us with regard to bank loans. I want to say categorically that my understanding of the position of the western farm organizations is that they regard this bank loan legislation not only as being ineffective but as legislation which discriminates against the wheat producer.
After the tremendous barrage of criticism made by the official opposition, and in particular by the hon. member for Prince Albert this morning, in respect of this legislation, I suggest that they should do what I intend to do as an effective protest, namely vote against this measure when it comes to a vote in this chamber.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce made certain statements. I cannot quote them from the record, Mr. Chairman, because they were made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. However, he said something like this. He said that recently there has been a drive for advances on farm-stored grain. Then he went on to say that the suggestion had been made that three-quarters of the value of the grain be advanced by the wheat board. He stated that many hon. members might think that this inspiration came from the farmers but that the fact was nothing of the kind, that it came from the cities. Then he went on to ask who were its supporters and said that its supporters were the enemies of the wheat board method of marketing. I have summarized what he said, but it can be found at page 127 of Hansard of January 16. I want to say to the house and to the hon. gentleman that if any group in the house should be ashamed of its record in connection

with the wheat board it is the Liberal party and the Liberal government.
I have a long memory and vivid recollections. There was only one Liberal member elected in the province of Saskatchewan in 1921, and that one Liberal member was the late Hon. W. R. Motherwell. I remember seeing the hoardings plastered with signs and a big sign stretching across the main street of the city of Regina saying:	"Vote for
Motherwell and the wheat board." At that time I was a member of the old Progressive movement which I supported until the movement disintegrated. I remember the fight for the wheat board all through those years. I remember how the wheat board came into being in the 1930's. that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure for the payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves owned by the Canadian wheat board in respect of board stocks of wheat in excess of one hundred and seventy-eight million bushels at the commencement of a crop year, such payment to be made to the board by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in form, this is a simple bill. In principle, it is of great importance. It is proposed that the government of Canada should assume carrying charges on stocks of wheat held by the wheat board in excess of 178 million bushels as of August 1, 1955 and that a similar obligation should be assumed by the government in each crop year until the board's stocks of wheat drop below 178 million bushels as of the first of the crop year. At that time, the legislation will lapse.
The purpose of the bill is to relieve the wheat board, and through the board, the wheat producer, from the burden of paying storage and interest costs on the abnormally large stocks which have accumulated in the hands of the board in recent years.
These excessive stocks have accumulated for one reason and one reason only-good rainfall on the prairies during the past 4 or 5 years. They are not due to excessive plantings of wheat. In fact, acreage is lower than

Wheat
it was 25 years ago. They are not due to subsidization of wheat production in any form. Prairie wheat growers receive exactly the price realized on world markets for their wheat, less storage and other expenses of handling and marketing. Unlike wheat growers in so many countries of the world, they have not cost the taxpayers or consumers of this country a penny in recent years.
Nor have these excessive stocks accumulated because of poor sales. In fact, during the period of accumulation of present stocks, export and domestic sales have been at record levels.
The cause of excess stocks is simply and solely good, well-distributed rainfall which produced a series of remarkably big crops, including the largest and second largest in history.
To all intents and purposes, the Canadian elevator system was filled to capacity on August 1, 1955, the beginning of the present crop year. At that time the Canadian wheat board owned 395 million bushels of wheat. The elevator system is likely to continue to be filled to capacity on August 1 next as producers deliver grain now on farms to replace grain moving into consumption at home and abroad.
The wheat board, therefore, faces the prospect of having to carry very large stocks of wheat for some time to come. Under the wheat board system of grain marketing, all carrying costs are charged to the producer who receives the net proceeds of sale, that is, the sale price less all costs.
The impact of increasing carrying charges first affected wheat board operations in the administration of the 1953-54 pool account.
Could we have a little order, please, Mr. Chairman?

I am going to ihave a few words to say about the opposition when I get through this more formal part of my remarks; make no mistake about that. I continue with my statement. This pool was under administration from August 1, 1953 to April 29, 1955. Carrying charges and interest came to 15-67 cents per bushel on the 398

million bushels of wheat delivered to the pool by producers. By way of comparison, if we look at the 1952-53 pool, the same items came to only 7-57 cents per bushel on producers' marketings of 533 million bushels.
The heavy carrying charges incurred in the 1953-54 pool would, of course, again be felt in the 1954-55 pool on which the board is still operating. In fact, it is estimated that the carrying charges incurred by the board in the administration of the 1954-55 pool might run close to 20 cents per bushel.
Under ordinary circumstances, there would, in my opinion, be no reason for the government and the general taxpayer to intervene to relieve the wheat board and the producer from any share of carrying costs. At the present time, however, I think there is a broad measure of agreement that it is in the interests not only of wheat producers, but of the country as a whole, that the wheat board should follow an orderly policy in disposing of its large holdings and not resort to panic methods of selling or giving-away. The experience of the 1930's is too fresh in the memories of all of us for anyone to suggest that attempts should be made to clear the shelves at any price. The frantic efforts to sell wheat in those years only produced price collapse. They did not sell any more wheat than could have been sold by orderly marketing. And extremely low wheat prices helped to aggravate and prolong the world depression of the early 1930's.
Aggressive but orderly selling is therefore in the national interest. If, however, the wheat board is faced with the burden of unusual and accumulating carrying costs for some time to come, it will be under the necessity of balancing price cuts against accumulating storage and interest costs. An assumption by the government of abnormal or excess carrying charges will therefore be a powerful aid to the principle of orderly marketing of wheat which this government supports.
This proposal may, therefore, be regarded as a contribution, and an essential contribution, to the stability of the wheat economy of the prairie provinces and an indirect contribution to the stability of the whole Canadian economy.
Over the period of 15 years prior to the harvesting of the large 1951 crop, average stocks of wheat in elevators at the end of each crop year was 178 million bushels. It seemed to the government that this was a fair gauge of normality. The 15-year period includes the low carryovers of the late 1930's, the high carryovers of the war years, and the low carryovers of the late 1940's.
The stocks of wheat on which the wheat board were paying carrying charges on

August 1, 1955 were 395 million bushels. Subtracting 178 million bushels, we arrive at a figure of 217 million bushels on which the government will assure the carrying charges during the present crop year. The charges themselves are in each case based on the last year's actual rates of storage and interest so that a figure may be arrived at immediately. The rates in effect on July 31, 1955 were equivalent to about 15 cents per bushel per annum. Therefore, the cost to the treasury this crop year will be about $32 million. What it will be in subsequent years will depend upon the level of board stocks, but it cannot go much above $32 million in any event because of the physical limits on storage capacity.
I believe that I have said sufficient to explain the government's reasons for introducing this legislation. The detail of the legislation itself, I believe, is self-explanatory.
The government has been urged to subsidize the western producer. It has been urged to subsidize exports and to resort to camouflaged forms of give-away. It has been urged to guarantee a minimum price considerably higher than the present initial prices.
The government has rejected all these proposals. It does not want to get into the business of subsidizing wheat production or exports as is being done in so many countries of the world, for this is the basic cause of the trouble in world wheat markets today.
The government does believe, however, that it is in the national interest that the treasury should help the producer over the present rough spot by carrying stocks in commercial storage above normal levels.
In due course, present wheat stocks owned by the board will begin to decline. When they fall to 178 million bushels, payments by the treasury will cease. If at some future time they should rise again above normal, it will be for the government and parliament to decide at that time whether there is any national responsibility. The present bill deals only with the situation now confronting the country and the wheat producer.
We have heard a great deal today and in recent days of what the opposition parties would do for the farmers were they in the position of the government. Well, now, there is a way of finding out what they would do. The surest way to find out what any man would do in a given situation is to find out what he did the last time he encountered this situation. Well, the government was active. We have heard a great deal about the Bennett government instituting the wheat board. The wheat board was not in action at that time but the government was in the futures market attempting to stabilize the price of wheat, and the prices grew lower day by day until wheat dropped to the lowest price in history. Mr. Chairman, before adjournment I had started to discuss the regime which was in power in this country from 1930 to 1935. There is much more I could say on that subject but as my time is limited I shall refer more particularly to Item No. 3. I may say that this method of assistance to farmers was decided upon only after I had attended the annual meetings of two of the three wheat pools, after I had discussed the situation with a great number of farmers, after I had attended a meeting of the farmers' union in Edmonton and after I had listened to a great number of proposals made by producers of wheat as to the best method of remedying a situation which was then and is now causing this government anxiety.
I have heard the suggestion that we should go on a two-price system, that we should charge the consumers of wheat in this country a higher price than we sell the same wheat for export. That proposal presents great difficulties. It would invite our customers abroad to ship their flour into this market and if we placed an embargo against their flour they would then say, "Why should we not put an embargo on against your wheat?" I should hate to make the decision that one section of the country should charge another section of the country a price which was higher than they would be willing to sell that wheat in any market except Canada.
Other proposals have been advanced from time to time, but after discussing the matter with the directors and senior men in the pools and a great number of members of the united farmers it was decided that the method of assistance provided in this bill would be the most appropriate and likely to be the most helpful that could be advanced for the purpose.
However, I think we should get back to business and I should like to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this da3r.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the committee is one of keen concern to everyone interested in agriculture in Canada, as well as those-and I know this would apply to all hon. members-who are interested in the economic prosperity of this dominion. I realize that there is some difference of opinion as to whether we should grant loans at 5 per cent to the farmers of western Canada or make cash advances on the wheat which they hold, wheat which the government in conjunction with the wheat board has failed to sell. I think that is quite a legitimate difference.
The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a strong argument in favour of guaranteeing the banks when making loans at 5 per cent, but it struck me as being rather odd that the farmers should have to pay 5 per cent when many others are able to borrow money for less. It is believed by all sides in parliament today that cash payments to farmers are necessary. The point is, why are they necessary?
For some considerable time I have listened to extensive debates on agriculture, and especially on wheat. Wheat production is an important branch of Canadian agriculture. We have been proud for many years of our No. 1 hard wheat. In fact I sometimes think we have been almost too proud; we thought that the world could not get along without it. I can remember discussions about its importance, and I think that is admitted by all.
Today we find our surpluses mounting until there are actually mountains of wheat in Canada remaining unsold. At no other time in our history have we known of surpluses of the size we have now except during 1930, when they were the largest in the 20th century up to that time. It is unique that as the great party which sits to your right were getting ready to leave office in 1930 they left
Grain
every elevator bursting with unsold wheat. Today at about the time they are getting ready to leave again, every elevator is filled with unsold wheat.
However, the minister has admitted that we have 100 million bushels of empty elevator space. As the hon. member for Prince Albert has pointed out, 100 million bushels of empty elevator space means that if that amount had been delivered to the elevators the farmers would have had $150 million more, and we would not need to be making either cash payments or loans at 5 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I have listened in this house for a long time, for nearly as long as any other hon. member, and it is passing strange to find that even though we have a tremendous increase in the production of copper and all other primary products, the one primary product over the sale of which we have had difficulty down through the years with this government has been this golden asset of agriculture, Canadian No. 1 hard wheat. Perhaps there is a relationship, because I have not in all my time in this parliament ever seen a government so smugly satisfied with itself, so sure that there is some other reason that we are in difficulty rather than any shortcoming of the government.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, with his characteristic optimism, says there is nothing wrong. He is more bullish than the greatest bulls on the market these days. He says there is nothing wrong. In fact he says he is rather happy about the situation. If we have too much wheat he says the reason is that it rained too much. The Minister of Agriculture sings "It ain't gonna rain no more" and says there will be no butter surplus because there will be no rain nex.t year.
Mr. Chairman, I sometimes wonder how the farmers of Canada can get such satisfaction, comfort or hope when they observe the policies of this government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us the other day that we have been selling so much wheat that the transportation companies cannot get it away as fast as they are selling it. He has told us that we sold 90 million bushels more wheat a year in the last five years than we ever sold before. Yet on the other hand he says, "If the farmers want it we will give them something; we will make them pay 5 per cent on it, because they are so well off that otherwise they will buy victory bonds and we will have to pay interest ourselves." Is it any wonder that they are starting to shoot up the public monopoly of television?
The farmers of Canada are dissatisfied. They have been dissatisfied in the past, but they are more dissatisfied today. I could name

Grain
cabinet ministers who know very well that what I say is true, but I will not embarrass them because any row they have in their own constituencies is their own problem. We have been told that we have had many more shipments and that the shipments had been going out rapidly. The hon. member for Prince Albert this morning showed conclusively what has been happening in that regard in the last few years.
We listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day. Experience must be the charm of the ages, because even with his short experience the Minister of Trade and Commerce almost made me feel that these mountains of wheat in western Canada were disappearing just like snowdrifts in a spring thaw. He said it might be an asset when we want it. I remember last year how he, speaking for the wheat board, said we might not have any bins full of wheat in Canada; we were to have it all sold, and probably there would be no wheat. What was a problem in January was likely to be an asset before July. Then the other day he said we sold 90 million bushels of wheat more each year for the last five years, and the only real handicap they had was the panic that was caused throughout the world by what the Leader of the Opposition had said about wheat.
I had realized previously that the words of the Leader of the Opposition are beginning to ring true. I realize that more people in this country are beginning to have confidence that we have a vigorous and forward-looking leader who will be the next prime minister of Canada. But I did not realize before that his voice was so strong that it would carry over into Europe and destroy the markets. As a colleague of his I am going to speak to him and tell him to be careful, because I am a farmer. I will try to get him not to say anything that might disturb the market for wheat. I agree with his policies in so many regards that I would not want him to upset the world wheat market by something he might say at this particular time.
The hon. member for Prince Albert this morning laid down in his characteristically clear style the true picture in this country.

from the farms in the 21 weeks from January 4 to January 16 were 65 per cent below what they were one year ago, and the deliveries or loadings overseas were 30 per cent less. Then on the other side, on the same day we find him saying that we must find money to support these poor fellows in western Canada. Yet we have almost one billion bushels-almost one thousand million bushels-on hand and they tell us that is not dangerous.
If you are in power long enough to build a halo of smug complacency and optimism around you bigger than a balloon tire, then you can say that these little things like a billion bushels of wheat are of no more concern than "what's a million" in your financial statement. These are things that the people of this country are getting concerned about. These are the things that are disturbing the farmers across this dominion. Some of us do not grow as many acres of wheat, but we try to grow perhaps more bushels per acre. There is not a grain grower, a cattle feeder, a grain seller or a grain buyer in agriculture in Canada today who is satisfied with the way in which this government is bungling, befuddling and bewildering the whole picture. The Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests that the minister for Prince Albert-

Oh, if we can only get the transportation and it does not rain too much we will solve the whole problem. It will be a great thing to have wheat. The Minister of Agriculture said a few years ago that we might have to eat it, and if we got into a desperate situation in a world conflict we could eat nothing but wheat and live on it for a time. In fact I have listened to very little else in parliament for 30 years.
But, Mr. Chairman, amidst all these blunders, bluffs and boasts these new apostles of trade experiments have created a halo of mythology among the farmers all across the dominion. If there is any compliment coming to them I compliment them on that halo around their heads which, as I have said, is bigger than a balloon tire. But what has it meant in reality? I have listened and I am convinced that they think that if you are in power long enough you cannot be wrong. In their opinion they exemplify democracy at its best. How they smugly smile and laugh, wisecrack at the opposition and say, "All is well because we did it."
Going back to the days of the past, by what yardstick do these giants measure their greatness? What yardstick are you using? Are you considering varying world conditions? Are you considering the changing times through which we have gone? Are you considering the increased world population? Are you considering the increased world production of wheat? Are you considering that last year the world consumed 117 million more bushels of wheat, yet Canada had very little more than half the proportion of that wheat
Grain
market that it had in the days of the Bennett government to which I belonged, and which the minister said sent abroad nothing but apples, cheese and so on.
I know what the western farmers will say today. They will say they have had nothing but applesauce for the last four years in western Canada. Yes, Mr. Chairman, where are these markets? What has this government done? I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar this morning and I listened intently because, while I have not always been in full agreement with many of his policies, he is one of the outstanding debaters in the Canadian parliament. He put the matter so clearly that if you did not believe what he said all you had to do was to look at the Minister of Trade and Commerce and you would know it was true.
He remembers what happened in 1935. May I tell you, sir, that, coming from the same part of the country as you do, I remember distinctly what has happened since 1925. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar gave me a lead. I had not intended to do so today, but I should like to review some of our past history to see where the merit or demerit of these giants lies in retrospect and in relation to other governments that have gone before.

I am glad there are those still in parliament who can review the true history of what has gone on in this country.

Grain
I can well recall what Hon. Mr. Motherwell had to say, as was mentioned this morning. I can go back further than that, to 1927 and 1928, when I pointed out the dangers that were confronting us. I remember a member of the Liberal party telling me, "You know nothing about western Canada. I am telling you, Rowe, you will never see wheat below $2 a bushel again." I said that from what I could see of what was going on in the wheat business wheat would be selling at 75 cents a bushel before he ever returned to parliament. When he saw he was going to be defeated the Grits gave him a job in the civil service, and later when he was free from politics he admitted to me on Sparks street that I was right and he was wrong.
These, Mr. Chairman, are some of the things that have happened. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not exactly in love with the Tories but he had sufficient affection for them that he was well regarded by them. Yet, Mr. Chairman, he now has the temerity to tell us what we did, that all we sent was cheese. He did not tell you the kind of mess we found. He did hot tell you that we were made the honorary pallbearers of the worst political mess Canada had ever seen.
No, Mr. Chairman, these things are not revealed, and perhaps I should not go back to them because I know that you, sir, as a younger man, feel that we older men should not talk about the days that are past. The Minister of Trade and Commerce would rather look to the future. He is the wild optimist who always looks to the future. His twin brother, the Minister of Agriculture, is afraid to look back and he is too cautious to look ahead. Where are the facts? Let me remind hon. members that the party now in power have not justified this halo of perfection they have built around themselves in smug complacency. Yes, Mr. Chairman, that cloak of smug complacency will be their shroud after the next election. It is true that they have skilfully advertised. Can the minister rise today and tell me about conditions in 1930 and 1931 which, as far as we were concerned, were a lot more difficult than they are today?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, his answer is just what I expected. His answer is that smug complacency which feels that a laugh or a grin is better than a silly answer. Yes, Mr. Chairman, I can take him and hon. members of the house back before 1930. I well recall what happened in 1925. Yes, I can remember when the wheat pool was organized. I can
TMr. Rowe.]
remember hearing Mr. Henry Wise Wood, and I remember the differences between him and A. J. MacPhail. I remember the speeches of Mr. A. J. MacPhail who, the minister will not deny, knew something about the picture and was very much concerned. Henry Wise Wood, who organized the pool, thought that wheat should never go below $2. What a lucky chance they had in 1924 and 1925. I remember distinctly being in western Canada when the billboards in support of Hon. Mr. Motherwell were as conspicuous to me as they were to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
Where did those who were out to kill the wheat board get their lead? Whose baby was it? They never fathered it, they never mothered it, and they even hesitated to adopt it. Right Hon. Arthur Meighen suggested it and then Hon. Mr. Motherwell grabbed on to it, much to the disgust of many Liberals at that time. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, he was elected by going contrary to his Liberal party. He knew more about agriculture than even the present Minister of Agriculture, for whom I have a great regard.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, let us face the facts. No one group in Canada, whether it is the wheat pool, the grain growers, the wheat board, the Conservative party or the Liberal party, has any monopoly on either the errors or the perfections of the past or present. We were told in those years that wheat would not drop below $2 a bushel. I can recall that there was a short crop in 1924 which allowed wheat to go up slightly to $1.96 per bushel. Then it was said the wheat pools had done a great job. They did not need the wheat board. They did not need very much help at that time.
Without reviewing too much of the past I want to come now to the 1930's and what happened. This government who now boast of what they have done about markets had practically lost the United Kingdom market for every important agricultural export we had at that time. I am not going to review the situation because the Minister of Agriculture knows better than the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we had lost our markets for dairy products, for meat and to a great extent for wheat. We found ourselves in 1930 faced with a smaller United Kingdom market than we had had for 75 years. When this government that sits to your right, Mr. Chairman, assumed office in 1935, we had the strongest British market, more stable markets, for products than we have had in 50 years.
Why had the earlier decline taken place? It was the result of the haphazard regard for agriculture that was clearly demonstrated here today when the government majority

was defeated by those who are concerned about agriculture. I am glad that the attendance is better this afternoon. I know hon. members are here because they do not want to be defeated, rather than hear me. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says he has tried to pick out the particular day when Right Hon. R. B. Bennett assumed office. At that time Mr. Bennett found this debacle: every elevator filled with wheat, every barnyard filled with cattle and every lumber yard filled with lumber. Canada was facing the greatest debacle it had ever known. Does anyone in this house think Mr. Bennett was powerful enough to create those conditions in three days? Why, three of these tired old gentlemen combined would not make a shadow of him.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce laughs, but he knows what I say is true because he was one of Mr. Bennett's work boys in those days. What did happen? Let me remind young hon. members who have listened to some of these hard-shelled old Grit campaigners tell about the squeak of Bennett buggies in western Canada, this mess was not created by R. B. Bennett. If we had not had as big a man as he was to clean up the mess, we would have been in a worse position.
What' did he do? He found this country full of unsold wheat. I know the minister was right this morning when he referred to the price of $1 per bushel. The average price of wheat was exactly the same the month Mr. Bennett left office as it was when he assumed office. I ask the minister, knowing all the bungling he has committed in times of prosperity, how he would have met these difficult problems in times of depression. During those years, between 1930 and 1935, when we were in power we had only 26 per cent of the world market. Yet when we went out' of power we had an average of 34 per cent. Today we have 5-5 per cent of the world's production and we are having more trouble than the Bennett government had with almost 9 per cent of the world's production.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that not a bushel of wheat was sold below the world price. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce said we would sell wheat at less than the world price. Where did he get that idea? Where did he hear anybody say that? The Bennett government never sold a bushel of wheat or recommended that the wheat board sell a bushel of wheat for less than the world price. Yet this government has sold wheat to the extent of $4 million
Grain
or $5 million less than the farmers in western Canada should have had. If they had that money they would not need loans today.
We talk about the wheat board. It is not our purpose to kill the wheat board. We created it. You have messed it up with Liberal socialism until even the wheat board does not know where you are going. The board is afraid to move. If one tries to find out what is going on in this wheat business, one finds it is like trying to peek behind a socialistic bamboo curtain. We are told we do not sell wheat for less than the world price. When I ask how much we sold it for I am told it is not in the public interest to give an answer. I am told we are trying to destroy the wheat board. We do not want to destroy the board; we want it strengthened by young, expert salesmen rather than have old politicians mussing it up.
You have laboured hard and long to create this myth that only you can sell wheat. Well, there is more wheat unsold than at any time in our history. You have cost the taxpayers $120 million. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was not here, but when the Bennett government took office the average price of wheat that month was 92 cents. Later a floor price of 87J cents was established. When we came into another crisis the Liberal government reduced the floor price to 80 cents. Then they turned around the next day and said, if we have to dump wheat we will do it as cheaply as anybody else in the world. In 48 hours the price had dropped 32 cents and was 60 cents where it had been 92 cents. Those are the champions in trade.
