Before we take a look at some modern history I may say that I agree with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) on one point. I fully expect to live to see the day when the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is the next Prime Minister of Canada, but I do not think that will be for another 20 or 25 years. I believe that once every 45 or 50 years the people of Canada should put in a Tory government for one term in order to be able to realize how good the Liberals were for the other 45.
Well, now, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has pointed to the gentleman who is sitting next to him, my genial friend the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I will concede right now, Mr. Chairman, that

Grain
in my estimation the hon member for Prince Albert is one of the finest criminal lawyers- I hope the Leader of the Opposition will not go out too soon because I am coming to a speech of his in just a minute. The hon. member for Prince Albert, I am frank to say, is one of the finest criminal lawyers in Canada, and if I ever do lose my temper and take a shot not only at a television set but at something more alive than that, and do unfortunately bump off someone in the opposition, I think that my first choice of counsel to get me off at the subsequent trial would be my good friend, the hon. member for Prince Albert. But when the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe suggests that the hon. member for Prince Albert could sell more wheat than is being sold under the leadership of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, I think it is a good idea to take a look at the record of exactly how the hon. member for Prince Albert said he would go about selling the wheat if he had a chance to sit where the Minister of Trade and Commerce now sits.
On March 25, 1954, as recorded on page 3339 of Hansard, when speaking in the debate on external affairs as the official spokesman of the Conservative party of Canada, he said we should not get rid of our surpluses, including wheat surpluses and other commodities. I am now reading from his speech:
The people in the western provinces and farmers generally in this country are asking what are the possibilities for agricultural trade. Some argue trade with the U.S.S.R. would afford a means of getting rid of our surplus farm products. What Is the attitude of the government with regard to this question? Has the government ascertained through its representatives in the U.S.S.R. that while industrialization has proceeded apace under the five-year plans agriculture has proven to be a failure?
The man who tells us how the Conservative party is to sell the wheat of Canada if or when that parity ever assumes power proceeds to say over on the next page:
Agricultural production has fallen to a level below that of 1928.
Then, a little further down-and this is the important point, Mr. Chairman-the official spokesman of the Conservative party, the man who would sell the wheat, said this:
I hope and trust that in return for the benefits of the present that are apparent in finding markets for surpluses Canada will not rush into trade with the U.S.S.R. and will give every consideration to the perilous possibilities inherent in contributing in meeting ferment in the Soviet union to which the Kremlin has found no better answer than more repression and the tyranny of purges.
Then, further down:
As to the question of trade, I fear that the economic advantages of the present will lure many to believe in the necessity or at least in the

attractiveness of trade with the U.S.S.R. on the assumption that we can restrict the things in which we trade to non-strategic commodities. In my opinion there is no more strategic commodity in the world than the production of agriculture.
In other words, if the hon. member for Prince Albert had to do with the selling of the wheat of Canada, we would not have sold the 1,000 tons of wheat that we sold to Poland last week; we would not even be negotiating with the Russians down-town in Ottawa today to try to sell a very substantial quantity of wheat. If the hon. member for Prince Albert had his way as the official spokesman of the Conservative party and the salesman in waiting of the Conservative party of the wheat of Canada we would not sell a single bushel to Poland, we would not sell a single bushel of wheat to any part of the one-third of all the world that now is so unfortunate as to have a communist government. We would have no truck or trade with the communists, exactly as the Conservatives advocated in the election of 1911.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say before we listen to any of the glib and shallow talk about the inefficiency of the present government in selling our wheat, or in not selling our wheat, we should look back to the clear-cut expression of policy on the part of the Conservative party which has until this day never once been disavowed as to how they would refuse to sell a single bushel of wheat, or of other surplus food, to any part of the communist one-third of the world.
Since we have listened so long and so generously at times in the past few weeks to how not to sell wheat, may I offer one constructive suggestion as to how I think we might sell it? I myself have travelled at different times for long periods in the countries of Asia. When I was in India in 1951 there was a near-famine there. Our trade commission was trying very hard to sell wheat in India. In my conversations with members of the Indian government I found them most reluctant to buy Canadian wheat if it meant the use of Colombo plan funds for that purpose. I also found that it is not just so simple as some members of the opposition sometimes suggest to dispose of wheat to two-thirds of the people who go to bed hungry every night. You must have some way of doing it. We had an instance of that in British Columbia not very many years ago. We wanted Canada to give some of our British customers apples. We actually offered them one million boxes of apples, but when it came to giving the one million boxes of apples to Britain we found there was no machinery to handle the gift. In the end the apples had to go to the people of Britain through the ordinary chan-

nels, of trade, and the only beneficiary, of course, was the treasury of the British government, which was all very well. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me we must have some practical suggestions as to how we might dispose of some of our surpluses beyond those that have been forthcoming. I would like to make two practical suggestions.
First of all I believe this government should send the most intelligent and alert salesmen that they can employ to try to sell wheat to China. I for one believe that if the Minister of Fisheries had not had that unfortunate accident, which resulted in the cutting short of his visit to China, something might have come out of his visit that would have led to a trade deal before now.
The second constructive suggestion I should like to make is this. I find that the great countries of Asia, such as India and China, have always lived on the borderline of starvation. They always live on the raw edge of nothing. There is always a small margin between the bare sufficiency which they ordinarily have and outright starvation. The margin is so small because there is no reserve. I believe it would be in the interests of this country, and of other countries in the western democracy, even if we had to put up a large sum of money, to enable those great countries of Asia to build up a sufficient food reserve, including a wheat reserve. Thank you.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the debate on this measure so far has more or less resolved itself into a question of whether this parliament should enact a bill which would be a guarantee to the chartered banks in the event that they should make some loans to farmers on farm-stored grain, or whether this parliament should move toward cash advances on grain. Up until this point we have heard a number of statements and speeches. Only this afternoon we heard speeches which reviewed the policies of previous governments, both Liberal and Conservative. It is not quite clear which party did more violence to the wheat board in its term of office, which did a poor job of selling wheat. I shall leave that to the people to decide. In the meantime, I intend to touch briefly on what I believe to be the opinion and attitude of the farmers in my own province of Manitoba. Manitoba seems to have crept into the picture rather dramatically in recent days. From what I hear, in that province those who view television really get a bang out of it. It brings back into the discussion the arguments that have been made by the hon. member for Rosthern in defence of the government's measure.
Grain
I think it can be summarized in this way. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in making what I would consider to be the main defence for the government in support of this bill made no attempt to argue that bank loans at 5 per cent were better, more sound or more realistic than cash advances. What he tried to argue was that what the government was doing represented cash advances and I think that is the main reason why his analysis of the situation and his argument in relation to it created so much heat amongst farmers on the prairies.
The farmers on the prairies, at least those in my province, do not mind being told by the government that in the government's opinion its considers bank loans at 5 per cent to be a better proposition than cash advances, and then proceed to argue from there. But when someone tries to shove down their throats something they know is not true it is an insult to their intelligence.
I am not surprised at the incident which took place the other day in Manitoba as reported in the press. A farmer on the prairies could read with some degree of equanimity the arguments presented by the hon. member for Rosthern and the other Liberal members as reported in Hansard. He might even be able to restrain himself when he listened to the voices of Liberal members over the radio. But when one of them intrudes not only his voice but his face right into the farmer's living room and argues in support of this resolution the farmer could only retaliate in a dramatic fashion.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am going to place on the record something which represents the attitude of the organized farmers in Manitoba. First of all a resolution was passed. As it happens, it was the first resolution to be considered by the annual meeting of the Manitoba farmers' union which was held in the city of Winnipeg on December 5, 6 and 7. This is the exact wording of this resolution which I think sets clearly before this committee what the attitude of that organization is. It makes no bones about it and it does not beat around the bush. The organization put it in plain language and I will put it on the record:
Cash Advances
Be it resolved that this fifth Annual Convention of the Manitoba Farmers' Union disapproves of the present system of bank loans to farmers on farm-stored grain, and
Be it further resolved that we request the Federal Government to make immediate provisions for cash advances to farmers on farm-stored grain on the following basis:
(a)	that these advances shall be the full initial payment
(b)	that these advances be paid on the basis of one-half of the deliverable grain
85B

Grain
(c)	that all administration and interest charges be borne by the Federal Government
(d)	that these advances shall be repayable on the basis of one-half the value of each delivery made by the farmer
(e)	that these advances be made through the facilities of the Canadian Wheat Board.
That resolution is very comprehensive and clear. It does not make any attempt to skirt the issue and it states exactly what the organized farmers, in the sense that they belong to that organization, are asking for so far as this parliament is concerned. For any member of the house from the prairie provinces, and more particularly from the province of Manitoba, to rise in this house and say that the farmers in Manitoba did not ask for cash advances or to say that what they are getting now can be considered as cash advances, is of course to argue against the membership of the whole of the Manitoba farmers' union which includes thirty to forty thousand farmers in that province.
I come now to the submission of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation. This was contained in a submission they made last December to all federal members from the province of Manitoba. I understand this same submission was made to hon. members of all the parties concerned. On page 7 of this submission, under the heading of "Cash Advances", we find the following:
Because of the current grain marketing congestion many farmers are in need of financial assistance. We most vigorously protest the payment of 5 per cent interest on loans against grain in store on the farm.
Now, that is perfectly clear. At best the government's measure provides temporary relief. The government of Canada has an obligation to the western grain producer. It should accept the greater risk in making interim payments on grain delivered. It should provide legislation for a long-term program for the financing of farm-stored grain.
The farmers who belong to this organization in many cases belong to both of these organizations because the federation includes all the co-operatives in the province. It is a well known fact that practically every farmer does business in one way or another with the co-operatives in Manitoba. Of course, it also includes a great many nonfarmers, those of us who are not engaged directly in agriculture but who do business with the co-operatives, and that probably includes a large percentage of the people in Manitoba. They are automatically members of the Manitoba federation of agriculture. Therefore these two organizations could be said to speak for practically the whole of the population of the province.

They have set themselves on the record very clearly on two points: first, they are opposed to the legislation which is now being proposed by the government, and secondly they are asking that cash advances be made. That is exactly what the members of this group have been fighting for ever since this session began.
As I said earlier, the hon. member for Rosthern and some of the other hon. members who are defending this legislation are attempting to draw a red herring across this whole argument by saying: After all, after the Saskatoon conference, the delegation that visited Ottawa and interviewed the cabinet or some part of the cabinet simply asked for cash advances and did not specify just how this should be done, leaving it to the government to decide this.
I am convinced, however, you cannot get away with that kind of technical weaseling out of the position the farm organizations whose resolutions I have quoted have requested as of December 1955. This can be backed by numerous other resolutions that have been passed in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. These groups have laid bare their attitude and opinions very clearly before the government and before this house.
Let us examine what the government is actually proposing. The resolution that is now before the committee has been described by hon. members of the government as a measure for providing for loans on grain to the farmers, but a careful reading of the resolution will reveal that it is nothing of the sort. Let me read it:
Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide-
To provide what?
-by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain.
This resolution purports to provide for short-term credit to grain producers but it does nothing of the sort. It envisages a bill to guarantee to the bank any money which the banks happen to lend to farmers who have grain to deliver. It guarantees nothing whatsoever to the farmers. There is nothing in this proposed legislation to say that any farmer who requires a loan or is eligible for one will receive it; it is left entirely in the hands of the banks. Therefore this resolution and the arguments advanced in its support thus far in the debate have been perfectly misleading. They have tried to create the impression that something is being

Grain
done to ensure that farmers will obtain loans when nothing of the sort is guaranteed by this proposed legislation.
Of course, I am not in a position to know what the exact wording of the bill will be but I have projected my imagination a little and I have written down what I think the bill will be when it comes up. Perhaps there will be a different version when it is introduced, for we do get different versions of things in this house, the Currie report for example. This is the kind of bill which would logically be written on the basis of what the resolution actually provides for. I have numbered it Bill No. CD-I and it is entitled "An Act for the Relief of Chartered Banks". The preamble and the sections, of which there are three, would read as follows:
Any similarity between this measure and cash advances on farm-stored grain is purely coincidental and completely ridiculous.
1.	Nothing hereinafter contained in this act shall be construed as guaranteeing anything to farmers. Any benefit accidentally inuring to the benefit of grain producers under this act shall be promptly reported to the Minister of Justice, who will forthwith put a stop to such nonsense.
2.	Should any farmer manage to obtain a bank loan under this measure, this unusual event shall immediately be reported to the Minister of National Revenue because such farmer must have an excellent credit standing and is therefore a good prospect for income tax boys.
3.	Notwithstanding any opinions expressed by farmers or their organizations or representatives to the contrary, grain producers shall take this measure and like it. (This order is pursuant to a decree issued by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, and shall apply mutatis mutandis to all future legislation decreed by radio and/or television.)
That is the only kind of bill that I can envisage that could logically be drawn up on the basis of this resolution. This resolution is not a measure to provide for loans to farmers; it is a measure to provide relief for the chartered banks of Canada, and any bank loans which might be made under it would of course be purely incidental.
One might think that I am expressing the opinions of the people of only one province, but I should like to add to what has been said about this whole matter what was contained in an editorial in the Star-Phoenix of November 10, 1955. Although I am not very familiar with this newspaper, I understand that it is not noted for being too unfriendly to the government. I hesitate to quote anything from the Winnipeg Free Press because recently the members of the government have become allergic to anything appearing in that newspaper. But I do understand that the Star-Phoenix has been fairly friendly to the Liberal party. Here is what they say:
Honesty and humility require us to admit that our comments on the federal government's emergency farm loan plan probably aren't nearly as
interesting as those made by certain politicians. But we take comfort in the thought that our arithmetic is less confusing.
Then it goes on to point out some of the arithmetic that has been bandied about in the province of Saskatchewan by some of the Liberal leaders. It continues:
For instance, Mr. A. H. McDonald was quoted as saying, at Moosomin on October 21, that a maximum loan of $1,000 per farmer at an interest rate of 5 per cent would be less effective than a stirrup pump at a forest fire. But on November 7, after the plan providing for a maximum loan of $1,500 per farmer had been officially announced. Mr. McDonald was interviewed in Saskatoon and expressed the view that the scheme would help the farmer who most needed assistance. Apparently $500 transformed a stirrup pump into a serviceable fire engine.
Meanwhile Rt. Hon. J. G. Gardiner has been arguing that, because the emergency loan is repayable on the basis of half the borrower's receipts from grain, as it is delivered,-
I want hon. members to note carefully the words from here on because they are in quotation marks:
-"by the time he has paid off the whole loan he has had $3,000 in cash to carry on with and has paid interest on half of it."
Those are truly wonderful mathematics. That is the end of the quotation marks and I hope that is not another one of those shameless misquotes. The editorial continues:
True, but he will still have borrowed only $1,500, at most-and if he hadn't taken advantage of the loan he would, by the same point in his grain deliveries, have had $3,000 cash with no interest to pay on it.
We don't think it helps anyone-least of all the politicians-to intimate that $1,500 is really $3,000, or that $500 makes a bad loan scheme into a good one. Whether the scheme is good or bad, the politicians are stuck with it. They ought to be devoting their attention now to the search for a more permanent solution to the farm problem.
I am glad that that last sentence was included in the editorial because that is exactly what the members of this group have been attempting to point out during this whole debate. Regardless of whether the government has its own way, which it appears to be determined to get now by pushing through this legislation in spite of general and I might say almost unanimous opposition by all farmers on the prairies, even if the government changed its mind and accepted the proposals made in this house by the C.C.F., and provided for cash benefits, even if they went that far, it would not provide a permanent solution to the grain problem.
We would still be in the position of having another crop coming along in 1956 and be faced with congested elevators, a shortage of box cars and all the things with which we are faced today. What is required is action on the part of the government in connection with selling grain and introducing marketing

Grain
policies which would be conducive to the sale of Canadian grain. Our tariff structure should be reduced in order to allow those nations which normally buy our grain to be able to send their goods to Canada and thus give the Canadian people the advantage of lower prices. That in itself would not only help our export markets but tend-this should interest the Minister of Justice-to reduce combines and monopolies in this country. The breaking down of trade barriers and the allowing of goods into this country would be the most effective way of doing away with monopoly and combines practices. It would keep our Canadian customers for Canadian grain and other agricultural products.
But if this government continues, as the Minister of Finance seems to be committed to continuing, a policy of restricting trade for the purpose of benefiting certain industries in this country rather than to allow trade to flow freely for the benefit of all Canadians, then we are going to continue to be faced with grain crisis after grain crisis. If the government has nothing better than this measly type of resolution to offer to the farmers of Canada they can expect greater and greater difficulties on the prairies.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the speech delivered by the last speaker brings up one or two matters which I think require a statement by me as Minister of Agriculture, coming as I do from the province of Saskatchewan. The province of Saskatchewan produces considerably more than half of all the wheat we are talking about in discussing these questions and therefore those of us who represent that province, whether we sit on this side of the house or on the other side, are very much interested in the discussion which is taking place.
I am sure we all agree that this is no question about which we can indulge in too much humour. I am not given to indulging in humour while speaking although I enjoy it when others use it, but on an occasion of this kind it is somewhat different. Neither am I so much concerned at the moment as to what brought about the conditions facing the farmers of western Canada apart from the fact that it is a combination of good crops and difficulty in delivering wheat to markets, even to those markets which we have available.
There has also been some difficulty in finding markets at this time for all the wheat that is available. Those are the main factors in connection with the situation which has developed. I only wish to say with regard to that matter that as a farmer in western Canada I am always more satisfied when
FMr. Zaplitny.l
we have a good crop than I am when we have a poor one. I am always more satisfied when we have more wheat than we can sell than I am when we have very much less than we can sell. I have gone through both experiences.
Some suggestion was made that at one time I favoured the grain exchange method of marketing. That is perfectly true. There was a time when we really did not have any other system but the grain exchange system of marketing. We developed from one thing to another until we eventually obtained the pooling system of marketing in western Canada. I have never been in favour of any other system but that one since it was first brought into being. As a matter of fact, I had something to do with stumping sections of the western part of Canada in putting it into being. I have had no reason to object to it or to oppose it since then.
I come down to this particular question which was all confined to one particular fact that existed last summer and last fall. The businessmen in the small towns and in the cities as well had been doing what they have always done in western Canada. They carried the farmer from the spring to the fall without any question whatsoever. When a farmer walked into their place of business and asked for oil, they gave it to him; when he walked in and asked for groceries, he obtained them; when he walked in and asked for clothing, he obtained it simply because they have always been accustomed to having bills run by these farmers over the years; and even in the years when we had to give them relief in order to get them by, the businessmen went to the very limit in order to see that the farmers were supplied. They did that this last season. There was an additional reason why they did it this last season.
Last spring we started off with the idea that we were not going to have very much wheat because we were not going to be able to get it seeded. It was raining too much. Then when we did get it seeded, growing conditions were so good that, as the summer advanced, everyone was of the opinion that we were going to have a good crop but that we might not get it off because it was late. Then when we came into the middle of the month of July, we had weather which ripened our crops much more rapidly than we expected to have it ripened. We therefore harvested a very considerable crop; it was the eighth highest crop we have ever harvested in the province of Saskatchewan and over all of western Canada itself, in so far as wheat was concerned.
I say again that the businessmen did not hesitate to give credit; but it can be said of

the farmers who farm in western Canada, they did not use as much of that credit as they had been accustomed to use over the 10 years since the war, the reason being that they had themselves very well equipped with machinery. At the end of the war they had little if anything with which to carry on. That was bad for operation on the farm, because they could not buy equipment during the war. But during the years up until this last year they had been equipping their farms and had them very well equipped. They did not buy as much machinery during the last year as they had bought recently, the obvious reason being that they were being careful in financing their farms. In spite of all that, when we came up to the months of October and November, the businessmen were looking for the cash that they in turn had to pay to the wholesalers here and there and to those who had supplied them with equipment from the eastern part of Canada and elsewhere.
So the concern was not so much concern on the part of the farmer as it was concern on the part of the businessman. He said, "Look here; I must have cash". The farmer said, "I have not got it". There could not be any argument about that. Whatever the reasons were, whether it was on account of car shortage or whatever it was, wheat had not been moving and the farmer did not have the cash. It would have been quite easy for some farmers to say, "It is not so much my worry; as long as I can go back to the businessman in the small town or elsewhere and get credit as I have always had it, I shall be able to carry on." Not many of the farmers said that, but they might have been justified in saying it. Instead they said, "Look here; these people have always carried us. What is going to be done about it? How are we going to get cash into our hands as soon as possible in order to go in and pay these men and let these men pay the wholsalers and others across the country and thus be in a position to carry on?" There was no one who had any idea in mind-the farmer, the businessman or anyone else- that any policy brought in at this time was going to settle all those problems that have to do with the marketing of wheat.
There are in this chamber members who, every time a westerner gets up to speak with regard to wheat, recall all the things that have been said over the last 30 years with regard to marketing wheat and who express the hope that the discussion will not be along the same lines. That is all right. But we are not attempting to settle the problems that we have been discussing over the last 30 years or that we are going to be discussing over the next 10 years or even the next year.
Grain
Here at the moment we are discussing only the problem that was involved in getting enough cash into the hands of the farmers who could not raise it otherwise in order to make it possible for them to pay their accounts in town, get their line of credit again and go on doing business as they have always done. If we can keep our minds on that particular question and deal with it, then we can discuss intelligently ways and means by which that may be brought about.
One of the ways, it is quite true-and the farmers do not hesitate to say so-would have been to get some variation of the old system that used to prevail before we had the wheat board at all. The farmers know-as do I and as do any other people who ever delivered wheat in western Canada-that there were times when a farmer went to the grain dealer, the elevator company and said, "I have wheat but I do not want to draw it in at the present time; I do not want to pay storage costs on it because the highest storage costs in the world are those in elevators. I want to keep it out on the farm and I will deliver it in due course". In those days the elevator company advanced 60 per cent of the value of the grain on the basis of the price on that particular day, and the farmer carried on. That procedure applied only to a certain group of farmers, farmers whose credit was perfectly good and about which there was no question.
Who decided that?
The elevator company decided that.

Did the
minister ever do that?

Yes; I have done it; but it is some time ago. I may say that anyone who could not do it was someone whose credit was not as good as mine, and mine was not as good as it is today. But we went along in that way. Some of us got help in that way. There are some people at the present time who can get help in that way. They do not need to go to the wheat board. They do not need to go to this government. They do not need to go anywhere except to the bank. When members on the other side of the house or on this side of the house say that there has been far more money lent outside of this plan than will be lent under it, they are only saying that the farmers of western Canada are in a little bit different position from that which they have been describing to this house.
A very considerable number of farmers in western Canada are able to go to the banks and get whatever money they require, a very considerable number of them have considerable wheat in their bins, and I am not going

Grain
to depart from the position I have always taken since I have been in the house and long before I came here that the best bank account any farmer in western Canada can have is a bin of wheat. That still remains the best bank account he can have. There have been no difficulties with farmers who, having bins of wheat on their farms, have gone to a bank and borrowed money, but every businessman in western Canada has had difficulties with people who were able to go to the bank and borrow money when they did not have wheat or did not have something else. They have had difficulties in those cases.
The situations of different people in the west have been described to the house a number of times. There is the young fellow, the chap who did not have any interest in land until a few years ago and then got it one way or another. One way was to go and buy land. Now he has payments to make. In other cases the father came to the time when he did not want to farm any more and he turned over his land to a son. When this occurs, nine times out of ten the young fellow makes an agreement with his father and sometimes with other members of the family that he will give them cash as a result of the crop he harvests. He will turn over cash to them. They usually make agreements based pretty much on everything that they are going to get or do. He will keep so much to run his own show. He will agree to pay so much to take care of his mother and father wherever they may be. He may agree to pay so much to keep a brother in university or someone else he is taking care of.
Then he comes to a fall like last fall and he is not able to market his wheat for the reasons that have been discussed here and he needs some cash. All this legislation says is that here we have a banking system set up in the country from one end to the other, a system that is looked upon as one of the best anywhere in the world and whose purpose is to serve the needs of a country like ours. That system is there. It is established. It is true that there is not a bank in every town but there is one in most towns and farmers who live near places where there is not a bank can go to a town where there is and get money by way of a loan.
That immediately suggested itself to everyone as the simplest way to arrange for the distribution of cash to the farmers. Other people came along and said, "Why not have the wheat board make advances?" A great many people who think there is some merit in that suggestion say that it could not be made to work so far as meeting this situation is concerned. It may be something you might

bring into effect at some particular time to deal with a situation that is there all the time but it is not the way in which to deal with this situation, and if you attempted to make it deal with it it would cost the farmers far more than 5 per cent in order to do it. I want to illustrate what I mean by that and the fact that this editorial was read a few moments ago gives me the idea that it should be said. When the farmers met and passed these resolutions at Saskatoon, in Manitoba and elsewhere they called attention to the fact that they thought half the money obtained from any wheat delivered during the winter months should be left in the hands of the farmer. It did not make any difference whether it was going to be advanced from the wheat board or where the advances came from. The indication was that half the money was to be left in the hands of the farmers.
In drafting this proposal the government said: All right, let us say a farmer wants $2,000. He has the wheat to use as security for the whole $2,000 and he wants the money over the next six or nine months until he gets into another crop year or until the wheat now in the elevators starts to move and he is able to deliver his wheat and get more money. Someone challenged us the other day to go out and have meetings in our constituencies. I had meetings in my constituency and I explained the matter to the farmers. What I said was this. I said, "If you want $1,200, go to the bank and ask for $600. If you want $2,000, go to the bank and ask for $1,000. If you want $3,000, go to the bank and ask for $1,500." That is what the editorial indicates I said. Then I said, "You can pretty well bank on being able in a few months to get some of your grain into the elevator and when you do put it in half of the money will go to pay off your loan and half will go into your own pocket to do whatever you wish with it."
I should emphasize here that with respect to these particular loans some of the things that have been said do not apply at all. The bank only has the government's guarantee provided they put the money in the hands of the individual and allow him to do what he wishes with it. You cannot get a guarantee any other way. To say he has got to do this, got to do that and got to do something else is all right if you are referring to ordinary banking but the banker cannot do it under this system. The farmer gets the money and the man who gets the money is told that he can go ahead and pay his accounts, take care of any indebtedness he has or use the money to live on during the period. But when he delivers wheat only half the money for that wheat goes on the loan and the other half is handed to him to do what he wishes with it.

How anybody can figure out anything else than that if the man gets a loan of $1,500 he is going to have the use of $3,000 over the period of the loan is more than I can understand. I should like to have it explained. He has got $3,000 in cash over the period to pay costs.
It is all very well to say that if he had not got it that way, if he could have got cash at the beginning of the season, he would have had the whole $3,000 and would not have had to pay 5 per cent interest, but I come back to what I said at the beginning. This was a set of circumstances that was there and had to be dealt with. It was not something about which you could theorize. The farmer needed the money, it was being provided to him and by next summer he will have had the amount of money I have indicated that is double what he borrowed.
I pleaded with them not to ask for too much in the way of loans because financing on loans has never been the best way for the farmers of western Canada. I just want to say this to him. I have been here quite a few years, but not as many as he has. I do not think that many sessions have gone by when I have not discussed wheat. I have been here just as long as I was in the legislature of Saskatchewan, and I discussed wheat there every year for about 20 years. In that time I, of course, have said a lot of things, many of them under circumstances entirely different from those which exist now. The remarks made then, therefore, cannot apply just in the same way as my remarks do now.
I am going to say to him that this story that has been told here by two or three with regard to the wheat board is not exactly

correct. The first wheat board we had was at the end of the first war, and that wheat board was done away with by the official opposition which became the government under Mr. Meighen. There was a very strong agitation in all the years from then until 1930 to get the wheat board back. In the meantime we had the wheat pools organized.
It is quite true that Mr. Bennett introduced a bill in 1935 to set up a wheat board. He had the greatest majority in this house that had ever been behind any government up to that time. He introduced a bill which provided for doing exactly what we are doing now. Well, Mr. Ralston, representing the Liberal party of that day in opposition, opposed it. He said we ought to set up a system under which we would have the right to deliver either to the wheat board or to the trade. Mr. Bennett could not get his bill through the house despite his large following. He withdrew the bill, appointed himself chairman of a committee, put Mr. Ralston on the committee with three others, and they drafted a new bill. The new bill was the one we had to put into effect when we came into office.
I quite agree that the Liberal party was responsible for that bill having been redrafted by putting up opposition to the former one; but I point out that the government could have put the first bill through if they had wished to. They did not wish to put it through. They had enough support on their own side of the house to put it through; but they put through a bill which gave a choice to the farmer either to deliver to the wheat board or to the trade.
It carried on in that way past the year 1938 to which my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar referred, when an amendment was moved and Mr. Motherwell rose in his place and opposed it, because it said that under certain circumstances the farmer could not deliver his wheat to the wheat board. But that is not the big question or the big point that we come to. The time of real choice was in 1943. In that year, in the middle of the war, every elevator company in Canada, including the wheat pools, came here and appeared before a committee of the cabinet, of which I was a member. In that committee they asked us to take over all the wheat that had been delivered to them and that had been paid for by them, and to take it over at the price of wheat that day, namely approximately $1.25 a bushel. We agreed to take it all over on one condition, that another pile of wheat would not be built up by the same elevator companies between then and the end of the war that we would have to compete with in selling our wheat.

That was the beginning of the compulsory board as it had been brought in first by Mr. Bennett, in 1935. I just wish to say the farmers in western Canada are agreed that this is the best system they have had. What the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other day was that some newspapers-one of them was read a few moments ago, published by exactly the same people who publish the Free Press, or which up to that time was published by the same people; now it is being published by another branch of the same family-were opposed to the wheat board. Well, if they can interpret that in any other way than that they are behind the strongest organization in this country that opposes the wheat board, I should like to have it interpreted for me, because I cannot understand it in any other way.

I was happy to learn that the other day one of the outstanding spokesmen for the Liberal party, the one who was on television the other day-I was glad he was not fired at in person but just his image; therefore he is still in a position to know what the people of western Canada are thinking-had this to say. The fact is that they lost between $300 and $400 million, and then the Minister of Trade and Commerce reluctantly gave them $65 million in settlement of those losses. That is how this government has lived up to its obligations.
One of the main bones of contention in western Canada is the tremendous interest rate being charged. I submit that it is a tremendous interest rate. That is what is causing the uproar more than anything else. That is the great difference between making loans through the chartered banks and having advances made. There is no organization that I know of that came out and asked for 5 per cent interest rates, yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that he went to western Canada to see what the need was and after hearing all these representations he ^decided that they wanted loans at 5 per cent.
"Mr. Gardiner: Did I say that?
?Mr. Johnston (Bow River): I doubt if any organization ever asked the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce for loans at 5 per cent. Will the minister answer that question?
IMr. Johnston (Bow River).]
I was just asking you when I said it.
I said I doubted if ever anyone asked you for that. Of course you did not go out on those visits with the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I always live on my farm for two to two and a half months every summer, and I was out there from the middle of July to the end of September. I heard those discussions.
You should get around and meet the people and not stay on your farm in between sessions. The rest of us try to get out and meet the people and find out what is going on.
About the only place I stayed away from was the by-election in Alberta.
You lost out on that one.

While we are speaking of this interest charge, Mr. Chairman, may I indicate to you what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to say about this matter as reported at page 127 of Hansard, this is what he said:
It has been said that the interest rate is too high at 5 per cent. I have been a borrower from banks all my life, and I have never yet succeeded in borrowing money from a bank at less than 5 per cent ... I therefore cannot be too greatly concerned about objections-
So he did receive objections.
But he is not concerned.

He said:
I therefore cannot be too greatly concerned about objections to guaranteed loans bearing an interest rate of 5 per cent.
Yet almost every organization in western Canada had sent a brief to the minister or had sent representations here, and protest meetings were held throughout the west by farmers' and other organizations. The minister disregards these things and he says, "I cannot be too greatly concerned about them".
I was not listening. Is the hon. member quoting me?

Does the minister object to that, too? I should not be surprised if the Minister of Agriculture objected to that because I would certainly object to it if I were he.

I may answer your suggestion by saying this. In the 40 years I have been in politics I have listened to everything

speechtext: You are the sum of all you have met.

I wish the Minister of Agriculture could sit a little bit closer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce so he could inject some of those ideas into him. If he could succeed in doing that he might improve the situation a little bit. A while ago the Minister of Agriculture was pointing out that in western Canada there was a need for these loans. But as to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, while he admitted that there was a slight need and that we were putting this legislation through for those few who were in necessitous circumstances, this is exactly what he said as reported at page 129 of Hansard:
Apart from that,-
And "that" refers to the storage price.
-it did not seem to me that there was any particular burden on the farmer through this condition of plenty.
If I may interpret that statement, I would say this. Apart from that, it did not seem to him that there was any particular burden on the farmer through the condition of surplus. I think that would be a fair interpretation of that statement. Yet the Minister of Agriculture disagrees with him strongly, as does almost everyone in western Canada. They disagree with him so strongly that they have protested in every way possible. It seems to me that the minister should have been fair enough, after hearing all these representations almost without exception asking for advances interest free, or if there should happen to be an interest rate, that it should not be more than 2 per cent.
That could have been done, and the banks could have done it if he had wanted to do it through the banks. They could have done it for at least 2 per cent or 2J per cent or 3 per cent. As I pointed out the other day, the province of Alberta made loans to their municipalities at 2 per cent, and they did not have the guarantee of the dominion government behind them. They never lost one penny on the loans. Surely if the provincial government can do that with their limited means of getting money, then the federal government with almost unlimited means should be able to equal the provincial government in that regard.
I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, that while we as Social Crediters strongly object to this legislation-and we have tried our
best and in no uncertain terms to convince the government that it is wrong and that it should change its policy-we realize the necessity, as does the Minister of Agriculture and as do the farmers in western Canada who need some assistance. We therefore intend to support this legislation, knowing at the same time that it falls far short of meeting the requirements or what was asked for by the farmers of western Canada and the various organizations there.
Just let me close by saying that I believe the federal government never intended that these loans would be of much use. The minister said he was basing his calculations on the 1951 loan, and in 1951 only 1,500 farmers accepted that assistance and there was a total lending of $625,000. That was because the interest rate was too high. Now over 2,000 farmers have asked for loans and they have borrowed over $2 million. In conclusion let me draw this inference. I believe that the minister never intended these loans to be used except in dire necessity, for this is what he had to say in Calgary on November 28:
It is my hope and belief that comparatively limited use will be made of the lending facilities, that most farmers are either in a position to carry on without borrowing, or are in a position to. finance in the ordinary way.
He never intended that they should use this legislation.

Did he receive representations from any other lending institutions asking the same guarantees as this legislation is going to give the banks? If so, what was the particular reason for refusing to grant that same protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes', there was a request from-is it the credit unions of Alberta?
If I may help the minister, it was from the government of Alberta through its treasury branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The difficulty was that we wanted the protection of the federal Bank Act. We could not obtain that if we used any institution other than the chartered banks. We were advised by our legal staff that the loans should be confined to chartered banks, and that course was followed.
I should like the minister to explain what he means by saying that they wanted the protection of the Bank Act. Does he mean the present government wanted the protection of the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is correct.

I wish he would elaborate on that a bit, because I do not understand how the government could have the protection of the Bank Act. As I see it, the position is this. The Alberta government asked for the

same guarantees that were given to the chartered banks. Whether there is any legal complication involved I do not know, but I would suggest that the refusal to grant the Alberta government the same guarantees would indicate that the chartered banks are in a better position than the Alberta government, and I do not believe that is so.
Then there is a further remark I wish to make. I do not know whether or not the Alberta government through its treasury branches would have lent money at a rate of interest less than 5 per cent. However, it is conceivable that they could have done so, and it is conceivable that other lending institutions might have been able to lend money to the farmers in this emergency period for less than 5 per cent. I cannot bring myself to believe that the minister and the government were not aware of that, and I do not understand why they insisted that guarantees be given to the chartered banks at 5 per cent whether or not the farmer could get money at a lower rate of interest from other reputable institutions. I doubt whether there is an institution in a sounder financial position than the government of Alberta.
These are the observations I wish to make. If there was another way of granting loans to the farmers at less than 5 per cent, why did the government not seek that way and attempt to alleviate the condition of the farmers to the extent of a reduced interest charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The guaranteed loans represent a comparatively small part of the loans that have been made against farmers' wheat. I understand that about $7 million has been lent under guarantees, and that close to $70 million has been lent by the chartered banks in western Canada. What interest they have charged on loans that are not guaranteed I do not know. I am perfectly sure that the government of Alberta is also lending money to farmers, and it is quite possible that my hon. friend is correct in saying that they lend at less than 5 per cent. I hope so. If that is the case, the farmers of the province of Alberta have the benefit.
However, the Bank Act is an act passed by this parliament. The guarantee is a guarantee given by this parliament. Therefore it was felt that the guarantee could only be given for loans through banks operating under the legislation of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it is a very fine thing that the debate on this issue has stirred the house to the extent it has today. I think it emphasizes the fact that serious injustice is being suffered by the people of the prairie provinces, and that the

members representing those areas are energetic, emphatic and determined in their efforts to bring this matter to the attention of the house in the hope that the government will do something about it.
Dealing with the situation in the few minutes I have left, I should like to start by saying we should all realize that the people of the prairie provinces, who form the backbone of the economy of those provinces, have suffered very severely not just this year but for a number of years. Some very excellent figures are available from the dominion bureau of statistics which show the terrific decline in net farm income. In 1952 net farm income in the province of Saskatchewan was approximately $565 million. In 1954, two years later, it had dropped to $126 million, a decrease of about $440 million. That is not gross but net income, and is a drop of about 77 per cent. As far as the farmers of Alberta are concerned, the drop there was about 50 per cent, and in Manitoba it was about 54 per cent. In the other provinces of Canada the worst decline was about 15 per cent.
I maintain that the position of the western farm producer is not understood. In fact it is misrepresented not only by the press of the country but sometimes even in the house. Hon. members should be made aware of the actual situation, which has not been presented properly. I was interested to hear the Minister of Agriculture say this afternoon that he was quite satisfied with what the present bank loan legislation had done. In the light of the position of the producers of the west the provision made does not amount to 10 per cent of what is needed. I would say that it only meets about 5 per cent of the actual and immediate need from which everyone in the west is suffering, not only the agricultural producers but the whole economy.
When these producers found themselves in an almost impossible position, tied hand and foot so they were almost unable to continue in operation, constantly harassed by debt, they needed something more than this and they asked the government for help. They said: We have the assets and we do not ask for a handout. Make it possible for us to realize some cash on the assets we have. We have just harvested one of the largest crops of the best quality grain. You have failed to give us box cars whereby we can deliver it. Our bins are overloaded. For heaven's sake give us advances on grain properly stored in our bins. If that is made possible then we can carry on. Every delegation from the western prairies and every representation made has made it known to the government that this is the minimum required to meet their need.
I should like to call it five o'clock.

I wonder whether I might crave the indulgence of the committee before rising to make a few remarks with regard to the votes that took place in committee today. This morning several members to my right entered the house while I was reading the question. In the vote in committee this afternoon several members to my left entered the house, I believe, while the count was going on. I do not wish to criticize those members in any way because there was considerable obscurity under the old rule as to the position with regard to entering the house or the committee during a vote. The old rule, as hon. members know, read as follows. It is rule 12 (2):
When Mr. Speaker is putting a question, no member shall walk out of or across the house, or make any noise or disturbance.
I must admit there was some obscurity in my own mind as well, because this morning I had forgotten that the rules committee and the house had changed rule 12 (2) to include the word "enter", so that the new rule now reads as follows:
When Mr. Speaker is putting a question, no member shall enter, walk out of or across the house, or make any noise or disturbance.
I was, therefore, inaccurate this morning when I said that while I was reading the question any hon. members who wished might have the right to enter the house. Under these circumstances I intend to say no more about the votes, and I think it might be fair and impartial to allow them to stand as previously recorded.
I have this suggestion to make, however, which would be, I think, of guidance to members and would certainly be of assistance to the deputy chairman and myself. It is this. When putting a vote in committee, just before the question I think I might say, "The question is the following", and at that juncture hon. members might kindly take it that the question is being put and refrain from entering the house. If this suggestion meets with favour, I think it would guide all hon. members and give us, shall I call it, a cut-off point at which hon. members would feel free to enter the committee or feel that they must remain behind the curtain.
I will say nothing more about it at this time, but I do feel that suggestion might prove of assistance in the future.
Progress reported.

the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Income Tax Act (corporation appeals).
He said: This bill, Mr. Speaker, is a companion one to the bill which was debated and voted upon in the house yesterday. The arguments for and against Bill No. 9 of yesterday are substantially the same arguments that would be used for or against Bill No. 10 which is now before the house. It is not my intention, therefore, to speak more than a moment or two in presenting this bill to the house. I present it despite yesterday's defeat of Bill No. 9 in order to give hon. members who may have repented of their action of yesterday an opportunity to redeem themselves by voting today for the lifting of the iron curtain of secrecy with respect to corporation income tax matters, at least to some extent.
Whereas yesterday's bill dealt generally with corporation income tax returns, today's bill deals only with the hearing of corporation appeals before the income tax appeal board. At the present time there is a subsection in the Income Tax Act, subsection 2 of section 92, which reads as follows:
An appeal may, in the discretion of the board, the chairman, the assistant chairman or hearing officer, as the case may be, be heard in camera or in public unless the appellant requests that it be heard in camera in which case it shall be so heard.
My amendment would simply add these words, "provided that if the appellant is a corporation the appeal shall be heard in public." In other words, just as yesterday we in this group took the view that corporation income tax matters are of public concern, and that the information in corporation income tax returns should be available to parliament, so today we take the view that corporation appeals to the income tax appeal board should be heard in public and not in camera.
As was the case yesterday, this bill leaves the matter of personal income tax appeals as they have been in the legislation. I remind hon. members, particularly those to my right in the Progressive Conservative party, of how anxious they were last year to get information as to who was the appellant in case No. 227 which was heard before the income

tax appeal board. The question in that hearing revolved around the desire of a corporation to get income tax deductibility for money which it had spent entertaining certain government people-we do not know what government-in an attempt to win contracts from that particular government. I remind my friends to my right that they were just as annoyed as we were that the information as to who that appellant was could not be obtained. This is their opportunity to say that hearings of that kind should not be held in camera but would have to be held in public.
So, Mr. Speaker, rather than give the house again all the arguments for this bill, since they were given yesterday in support of Bill No. 9, I rest the case on the basis of yesterday's arguments and the additional remarks I have just made. I urge hon. members to take this opportunity to vote for a lifting, in part, of the iron curtain of secrecy with respect to corporation income tax matters.

speechtext: The business reserved for this hour having been disposed of, the house will now revert to the business which was under consideration prior to five o'clock.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for shortterm credit to grain producers in the prairie

Grain
provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain; to provide also that the governor in council may extend the application of the act to cover loans made before the 1st day of June, 1957; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the act be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Before time was called at five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was referring to the matter before the house under this resolution, and I was outlining why we were opposing this resolution, what the position of the producer was, what his requests were, why they were made, the government's offer, and what we think should be done.
This being assistance to the western grain producer, an opportunity to borrow money from the banks with the government guaranteeing those loans, people will wonder why it should not be considered as something of value. It is admitted that perhaps it is of a little bit of value. A 5 per cent loan may be a little bit better than a 6 per cent loan. We protest that the whole thing is inadequate and that even the loans, such as they are, will not take care of the situation which exists with respect to the producers there at the present time.
We are opposed to this measure because we think it is impracticable as a means of dealing with the situation. We think it is unjust. We oppose it because we believe it is wrong in principle to ask these people, who are in the position in which they now find themselves because of the actions of this government and the administration of this government-they are tied hand and foot and are unable to move-to go to the banks and make these loans and pay interest at 5 per cent on the money they borrow. This provision is niggardly and completely inadequate in the face of the need that exists, and it is not going to help those who need it most.
The farmers have asked for cash advances. Every organization has let the government know that cash advances are what the farmers need. The farmer with thousands of bushels of good grain in the bins on his farm has an asset. He should be allowed to deliver it. He is not allowed to deliver it because box cars are not available. There is some space in the elevators but there is not sufficient space to take care of the whole crop. But he says; I will hold this grain. You can, if you wish, come and inspect it, grade it in the bins, arrange to have a padlock placed on the bins if you like, as is done in the United States where similar loans are made. Enter it in my permit book against any deliveries which might be made in future; let them know that you have allowed me to have the money in advance for the assets which I have. As soon as I am permitted to 67509-56i
deliver, you can deduct from my deliveries those advances which you have made. Surely such a request is not out of line with what should be granted. It is a relief to the farmer. It would be a relief to the whole economy.
If the government is responsible for the condition which exists, surely the government should be willing to pay the interest cost. They can get the money much more cheaply than can the farmer. Certainly the farmer does not feel it is right that he should be asked to pay 5 per cent on these advances. I will tell the government this. If they will let the farmer deliver his grain; if they will open the delivery points and get box cars so the farmer can deliver his grain, the farmer will be satisfied. That is all he is asking. Let him deliver. Then there will not be any demand for this kind of legislation. The whole economy is tied up because of lack of cash. Under the circumstances the farmer is surely not asking for something that is not right.
I find it difficult to convince people in this part of Canada of the situation that exists. I am surprised at the lack of knowledge on the part of people in the east with respect to the actual situation. The misunderstanding of the farmers' plight in the west, in my opinion, often stems from reports that appear in the papers about the condition of the farmers in the west.
I should like to give an indication of the kind of thing that I find in newspapers in the east which is a misrepresentation of the case. The other day I ran across an article in the Hamilton Spectator by H. M. Halliwell entitled "Prairie Letter". This is what this person has to say about the case of the western farmer:
Just who is this fellow, the wheat farmer and what Is his case against the rest of the country that he feels he should be helped? Well, he's a man of many parts. He's a big operator on, say, two sections of land or more, all paid for. He has a full line of implements, probably a house in the nearest town or city where he spends part of the winter if he doesn't go south or west, and he probably has 20, 30 or 40 thousand bushels of wheat in his bins to borrow money on if he can't sell it or protect him against crop failure.
This portrayal of the situation is entirely wrong. I remember a cartoon in one of the Ontario papers last year at the time we were suggesting that the situation of the prairie farmer was getting desperate because of the drop in net farm income and the constantly increasing cost of operation. We said that the first thing the government knew the farmers of the west would be marching on Ottawa. The cartoon that appeared in the paper showed the western farmers marching on Ottawa with the parliament buildings in the

Grain
background and a wide roadway in front. The roadway was lined with Cadillac cars and the western farmer was depicted with a ten gallon hat and a big cigar in his mouth. On the side of the cars were signs saying that on his way back from Florida he was marching on Ottawa to ask for help.
These are the kind of things that give an entirely wrong impression of the actual situation. Do the people of the east realize that the net income of farmers in the province of Saskatchewan alone has dropped by 77 per cent since 1952? It is true that in odd cases money was made in some areas of the province a few years ago when farmers picked up tracts of land cheaply and planted a crop, but that does not represent the average position. That is not the condition of the farmers today. With that kind of drop in their income something must be done. Surely any fair-minded person in the house will realize that a situation exists which requires action, and that is what we are asking now.
The request of the farmers was for cash advances. The misunderstanding of the farmers' position is, unfortunately, aggravated sometimes by statements made by cabinet ministers and sometimes by people representing the west who came down here. You will see reports in the newspapers that the farmers of the west were never so well off in their lives and never had it so good. That condition may have existed three years ago. Today the average farmer on the prairies is in desperate circumstances, and that is why he is protesting.
The reason the farmers of the west are opposed to the proposal of bank loans at 5 per cent is that such a provision is inadequate. When loans were first proposed he was told that this was a great solution, and that he was going to be allowed to borrow money from the bank. Some farmers have to travel 40, 50 or even 60 miles to get to a bank. I talked to one farmer who went to the bank. A number of people were lined up ahead of him and he had to wait for three hours in the bankers' outer office before he could see him.
When he did get in he had to fill out a loan application form. The name of the bank has to be filled in and the farmer has to give a complete report almost the same as in his permit book. He has to give particulars of land owned and land rented from others. He has to estimate the quantity of grain that will be available. At the bottom of the form there is this provision:
In order to qualify for guarantee the amount of the loan must not exceed one-half the dollar amount inserted in paragraph 5 or $1,500, whichever is less . . .
He has to make all these entries that are made in his permit book. Then he has to make an estimate of his financial worth in accordance with the statement of affairs on the bank's form, and then fill in particulars of all liens or other claims. The bank manager tells me that after an application for a loan is received he has to sign the following certificate at the bottom of the application:
I hereby certify that I have scrutinized and checked the foregoing application with the care required of me by the bank in the conduct of its ordinary business, and that at the time the loan was made the borrower produced to the bank the above-mentioned permit book for the farm described above and endorsed therein a direction as in form "GB" that one-half of all moneys payable in respect of grain delivered by him or on his behalf under the permit book be paid to the bank until the loan is repaid in full, and that to the best of my knowledge the terms of and conditions in accordance with which the loan was made are such as to qualify it for guarantee by the Minister of Finance.
The bank manager has to sign that certificate. He also informed me that his instructions required him to write to the secretary of the rural municipality in which the producer lived to find out whether there were any tax liens against the property or the grain held there by the farmer. He also had to write to the court house and have a search made to find out whether there was any other lien against the property or the grain. He also had to write to the Bank of Canada branch in Regina to find out whether there were any other encumberances against the farm. He said that it took weeks sometimes to do all this, and that there was great delay.
Not only was the value of the grain held by the farmer reduced by one-half, but the value of any grain which the farmer might have delivered was deducted from the amount of the loan that could be granted. Any arrears of taxes also had to be deducted, as well as any other encumbrances. The result was that the loan a man could receive from the bank amounted to very little. This extra security was required, but the only farmers who could get a sufficient amount to be of any help had to have such an amount of assets in the form of cattle, acreage and so on that they could get a loan from a bank anyway without all this trouble.
I should like to call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
